en: Salutations to that Bhavānī, who is skilled in destroying the miseries of worldly existence, who is Śāradā, and who sits upon a white lion-throne like an autumnal cloud; salutations! (Bhall 1)
May those first rays of your sun, the jewel of the sky, which possess the glow of rising, bestow auspiciousness upon you—
those rays which, during the great festivals marking the birth of day, make the quarters of the world appear like women with faces reddened by vermilion.
Since words are bound by the essence of dedication after first undergoing thorough refinement, why would they not immediately yield those intended meanings?
Like thieves who are exceedingly soft-hearted, the words of great poets surrender even unintended meanings by force.
Those for whom glass is a jewel and a jewel is glass are indeed other embodied beings;
those for whom glass is glass and a jewel is a jewel are the truly wise.
Indeed, O Kālakūṭa, by whom was this ever-increasingly exalted station of yours taught?
First you dwelt in the heart of the ocean, then in the throat of the bull-bannered Śiva, and now you reside in the speech of the wicked.
A treasure in times of distress, an ornament in festivals, a refuge when one is afraid, and a lamp in the night—
a certain true jewel like you is capable of bearing the burden of manifold benefits.
The goddess Śrī, like a wanton woman meeting her lover in secret, proceeded along paths darkened by thick gloom;
she was unable to endure even the mere sound arising from the ornaments of those possessed of merit.
Pride has departed; Modesty restrains her from seeking tranquility; Shame scratches the earth; Independence turns away and stands still; and Fortitude has fled, shaking off its hands.
O Thirst, this is the only fruit obtained by that person who followed after you: he whom you once touched with your foot now refuses to allow anyone else to touch his feet.
Let him fall into water, let him go to another quarter of the world, let him enter fire, or else let him go to the earth;
even so, what loss is there to the virtues of this sun, which cause wonder to all the world? (Bhallata 9)
Behold how those of virtuous conduct, who discern between the real and the unreal, describe this [sun]:
whatever thieves, unchaste women, and the like say of it is accepted; if that were accomplished by the sun, then he would be a true doer.
The setting of the sun leads to great glory, not to affliction; for when the time has come, who here has not gone, does not go, or will not go to their rest?
But this alone causes exceeding pain: that these darknesses, excluded from the world, have found a place even in that very sky which is vast by nature.
*VAR: {vāstam/lem /Mah; vāntam / ed; cāstam / H/A, cānye /K}
Let them enter the row and be counted in reverse order, or let them be ashamed even by this much;
for even the virtuous appear like the non-virtuous when the light of the sun veils the sky, as do the moon and the other luminaries.
Now that the sun has departed, the moon will not experience the improper pain of separation from the awakening of the three worlds; therefore, there is nothing more incomparable than this:
that these lamps have arisen here, their flames intent upon the destruction of the darkness, producing even greater heat for the heart.
That which does not touch upon the actual meaning, even when applied to the moon rather than the sun,
was given as the name "firefly" for an insect by someone who was pleased.
O jewel-insect, now that the day has come with its beautiful white rays veiled by the sun’s beams,
your shining in the night— when the ten directions are soiled by thick darkness— is quite another matter.
May no well-being come to that pitifully deluding fragment of light, which flickers within living beings or consists of a hollow superimposition of qualities;
for by this insect called a "firefly," which sparkles with a glow reddened by the spreading of its own shadow, we are mocked by the false notion that it is a moving jewel.

Only an elephant knows the agony of being struck by the continuous blows from the spears and tusks of another, as it shatters the towering mountain; the jackal, whose movements have ceased upon hearing the mere growl of a puppy, does not know the pain of falling into the cage-like claws of a lion.
Let this young *cātaka* bird now offer its supplication to its own head, which is afflicted by excessive height;
for if it so desires, where indeed are those waters—clear, cool, and sweet—not to be found throughout the vast quarters of the sky? (Bhallata 18)
That unprecedented inversion of the tongue, that fickleness of the ears, and that gaze which has forgotten the distinction between self and other due to intoxication—what more need be said?
O bee, since you have concluded thus that the elephant even now remains with its trunk empty within, brother, what is this obsession of yours?

Such is that cleverness to distinguish the true nature of milk and water as they are rightly mixed; such are your conversations and that graceful charm consisting of the pleasant placement of soft words.
Let it be, O crane; even if you know something of that sort, my friend, how is it that you, with your drooping shoulders, do not remain silent like a swan? 20.

Seeing a jar of fresh curd fallen on a deserted path, uncovered before those who have no protection, if the one-eyed crow—puffed up with pride, his neck held high, and agitated by hundreds of transformations—does not perform his various natural antics, when indeed will he ever do so? (Bhallata 21)
*VAR: {elevated/lem/ed; uprooted/Ka}
These peacocks are seen dancing charmingly, and these parrots are reciting melodiously; yet they are not even noticed here, or rather, they are driven away in anger.
For now this deceitful crow, having gained access by announcing the arrival of a beloved traveler to the woman of the house, devours this [food] without restraint.
O camel, you wish to howl like a jackal; alas, what a fever for your ears! Or rather, your own long neck is your refuge;
weary from the movement of its many joints, it will utter speech only after a long time.
At such a moment, who knows what will happen to whom?
With so many internal cavities and so many thorns on the outside, how could the fibers of the lotus stalk not be fragile? (Bhallata 24)
What is the reason for your covering these very long, white lotus-fibers?
For if a noble person sees them, Fortune, as if terrified, will not set foot there.
There is no birth from the mud, nor a fondness for dwelling in water; your body is anointed with a luster that steals the brilliance of the gems of the land-lotus.
If the ill-fated Creator had not made you light of heart, you alone would have become the supreme abode of Lakṣmī in this world.
Let the peacock, having climbed a tree on the path, cry out loudly for a long time; yet when the quality of sound pervades all directions, the conch shell remains the object of true esteem.
A conch shell, reduced to mere bone, cracked or dead, is made to breathe by the breath of another;
yet truly, only that sound which issues from it is audible, and not every sound that does not proclaim a true purpose. (Bhallata 28)
O Mother, alas, where have those trees gone— those that were so rich in sprouts and flowers, so abundant in flowers and fruit, and so lovely with the excellence of their fruit?
It is indeed well that the Creator did not labor in vain in its creation;
for what is the use of sandalwood fruit that does not correspond to its own nature?
This great fool, the sandalwood tree, having been climbed by venomous serpents bound together with mutual chains, is not resorted to by flowers; for this very reason, it is deprived of fruit.
We tolerate venomous serpents upon the sandalwood tree because it is a beautiful object left unprotected;
tell me, O Khadira tree, have you gathered your thorns merely to preserve your own dignity?
Whatever is improper, even if it follows the conduct of the proper—has the sandalwood tree not produced flowers or fruit?
We feel ashamed as we approach its presence, carrying great axes in our hands from the very start.
"Has this been obtained after a long time like nectar? Will it lead to immortality, or will it even bestow a long life like a medicinal elixir?
This is its fruit: that this wicked, stubborn palm tree, scorched by the curse of the traveler, bears fruit only after a hundred years. (Bhallata 34)

That sandalwood tree, which was your satisfied friend, has been cut down; you have fled and arrived here, and those pleasures of habitual enjoyment that you experienced there have been forgotten by you every day.
O serpents, if you do not retaliate against that attacker with the fiery venom from the tip of your fangs, why did you not yourselves go to pieces along with him?

Is it contentment? Is it incapacity? Or perhaps a lack of appreciation for him? Is it greed, or this instability, or even hatred? Let it be; O Fickle Fate, why was the sandalwood tree not joined with a flower that was at least worthy of it, even if it were not fruitful? Why was it not united with a blossom that was at least appropriate, however unproductive? Bhallata 36.
Why were you born at a crossroads? Why do you possess such dense shade? Why are you endowed with fruit-bearing branches? Why are you laden with a weight of fruit?

Why are you bent low? O noble tree, my friend, now endure the pulling of your branch-tips, the shaking, the crushing, and the breaking caused by the people through their own loud cries and wicked deeds.

"Rooted in goodness, renowned for its height, possessing dense and shining foliage, standing on the path of the virtuous, and worthy of being resorted to by the good"—considering this, the traveler took shelter under a palm tree.
Yet, such is the power of man: it may bear fruit today, or tomorrow, or at some time in the future, or perhaps never; but Fate alone is the master. (Bhallata 38)
At your base, this entire human lifespan has passed while my body withered away; beyond that, how could there be even a moment’s power to live?
Therefore, may it be well with you; attain great growth. O auspicious one, what haste is there for us even now?
You have already borne fruit, O palmyra tree!
Or among sons or grandsons. // Bhall 39 //

"Let us see what he will do"—thus thinking, the ministers, who had long neglected him out of pride because his ritual practices for attaining supernatural powers were so meager, were now driven by powerful karma.
Having gained full scope for their influence and being unable to restrain him, alas, that vast mountain village was consumed by such a formidable enemy, like a forest fire unleashed by a dense cloud.
Excellent, O cloud of sudden onset! Excellent, this which is to be meditated upon by the wise on this earth! Who else is capable of performing such a difficult task?
For while there are only a few fields suitable for all [crops], there is lightning upon them; whereas in all the forests of burning sand that are unsuitable, there are showers of water.
Let us set aside the distant possibility that your rain might provide some benefit to a thirsty wild ox, a bird, or any other creature;
but look, even for this desert wasteland of a cloud—which is utterly unworthy of it—has its scorched surface not become even more harsh again and again? (Bhallata 42)

O Ocean, you who have abandoned other waters fit for drinking and rinsing the mouth because you desire to serve him—do you not feel shame before people for your waters used for such base purposes? 43.
This ocean, well-known even to women and children, is kept at a distance by those who thirst for it simply because it is undrinkable;
why then does it further terrify others with successions of waves made formidable by rows of sea-monsters with jagged fangs?
O Ocean, why do you distress the cavity of our ears by crying out on all sides with deep and heavy roars that praise your own greatness?
For here was born from your jar a single crest-wearer (Śiva), who, though desiring to drink, was unable to hold even a single mouthful of all your waters.
In the three worlds, this quality of being the support for all waters belongs to you; furthermore, this splendor of the ocean, the abode of waters, is your very essence of great being.
For, having encountered you—who are terrifying with your many waves—the conflict of thirst and heat is extinguished somewhere in the current over the stones of the coastal mountains.
If you do not feel agitation, and if you are attentive enough to lend an ear for a moment, I ask you something, O Ocean; having reflected upon it, give me an answer.
When thirsty travelers, restrained by an extreme intensity of despair, look upon you only after sighing—how much greater would that [suffering] be than the Aurva-fire?
What kind of purity can there be for that insentient crystal stone, which is split within by an adventitious condition according to one's whim?
"O wish-fulfilling gem, do not despair, my friend, thinking that no lord on earth has ever borne you upon his head;
for indeed, there is no one here whose noble head possesses the good fortune or the seed of merit required to support you. (Bhall 49)
If there is consciousness, then qualities appear in the world; for that is what is praised here. So, what can be said?
Indeed, O Sumaṇas, roll about right here for as long as you live, you who are the very body of my discourse on the conquest of the world! (Bhall 50)
By what means did the Creator make this quality of being a "jewel" equal for both the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and the grass-gem (*tṛṇamaṇi*)?
One does not grow weary while granting the desires of supplicants; yet the other feels no shame in accepting a mere fragment of withered grass.
To some he is far away; some of unrefined intellect do not know his inner nature at all; some proud person does not beg of him; and some of meager aspiration seeks only a trifle.

Thus, for this Cintāmaṇi who is addicted to the vice of granting whatever is requested, there has been no testing ground—bright with the lines of magnanimity—in those places of trial that are difficult to cross due to lack of skill.

He who undergoes suffering for the sake of others, whose very breaking is sweet to everyone here, and whose transformation is indeed desired by all—if he does not reach full growth, is this the fault of the sugarcane for falling on barren soil, and not rather the fault of the desert land which lacks virtue? (Bhall 53)
Are there mango trees with heads bowed under the weight of their fruit? Are there lovely plantain trees that provide shade and dispel the heat? Are there fragrant, blossoming campaka trees?
These are merely *śamī* shrubs, half-grown after being licked by fierce, unrestrained camels. O fool, why do you wander in vain in this windless desert, only to die in vain?
O base-born dust, if you have performed even the slightest act of merit since your birth, then speak of it yourself!
For what purpose were you raised up by that wicked fire-charioteer? Now fulfill that purpose and defile this entire world!

Lacking substance and exceedingly light by nature, these withered fragments of old grass and the like, which were not fit for any task and had been blown away by the independent wind today—alas, look! By that very same wind, now turned inward toward its own core and utterly unsteady, they have been hurled into the sky above the great mansions.
Those particles of dust which were always light by nature and never counted anywhere, which were daily trampled underfoot and long remained hidden in the earth—
behold, now, when tossed upward by the fickle wind, they occupy the highest positions in the sky, acting as mountains above the lofty peaks.
O biting serpent, it is true that the Lord, out of affection, leads even you—an unworthy one—to the place of the anklets;
yet do your fainting jingles, accompanied by the humming of swarms of bees drawn toward them, serve only to bring about your own destruction?

In one case, there are excellent jewels upon the head, the home is a mountain cave, renunciation is one's very skin, and sustenance is effortlessly provided by the winds; such is the conduct in one place.
In another, the path is crooked, the tongue is double-tongued, and poison is seen in the gaze—fie on that! Yet, O friend serpent, a lamp burns after it; what indeed is this?
O abode of sea-monsters, do not despise these jewels because of the harsh blows from stones tossed by the great waves;
was not even Puruṣottama himself made to stretch out his hand in supplication before you because of the Kaustubha gem? (Bhallata 60)
He has many mouths, his great vital breath is indeed well known, and his offspring are the serpents; yet when he is provoked, one must consider how this world exists.
Such is the wondrous conduct of Śeṣa throughout the three worlds, by whom that wicked behavior characteristic of his kinship with poison-eaters was, as it were, wiped away and brought to an end.

Throughout the entire year, each day is praiseworthy in its own way; yet this particular day is unique, for it is conducted with such greatness by people that neither those who came before nor those who follow can equal it.
If a dog, its shoulder-blade made bristly with bound artificial manes, is elevated to the rank of a lord of beasts,
how could it ever produce the roar of the king of deer, who is intent upon splitting the temples of rutting elephants?

O cruel one, is this befitting of your purity, consistent with the elevation of your own side, appropriate for the ripening of your fruit, or worthy of your devotion to virtue—that while you have approached the vicinity of the ear for a moment, you fall with a cruel arrow upon those standing before another from afar? (Bhalla 64)
Indeed, these who are seen here possess truly auspicious forms; their beauty bears fruit when they come within the range of one's senses for even a moment.
Alas! In this world shrouded in darkness, how is it that this eye has now become equal to all things, or rather, not equal to other parts of the body? (Bhallata 65)
When birds are summoned, the mosquito does not come forward even when warded off; though dwelling in the midst of the ocean, the firefly-gem possesses the luster of jewels;

and even the glowworm does not tremble to move among the luminous bodies—fie upon this insentient commonality, which, like a master who has not discerned the inner truth, remains oblivious to its own nature!

O wise goldsmith, homage be to you! For, in order to examine it many times over that which is difficult to test, you place this golden ornament upon the scale as if it were equal to a common stone. (Bhall 67)
That dark well, the jar, has indeed already perished, being incapable of even receiving your grace;
yet you have sealed its base conduct by accepting even a single drop of water from its mouth.
In truth, what vastness of intention can be attributed to both a grass-gem and a human being,
when the grasping and the giving away of each are respectively concluded by a mere fragment from the tip of a slender blade of grass?

If a centipede, despite possessing a hundred feet, is unable to traverse even the footprint of a cow, do we on that account dispute the crossing of the ocean by Hanuman, the two-footed one? (Bhallata 70)
There is no proficiency in maintaining the lineage of gurus, nor any regard for gathering great virtues;
even the talk of bestowing fruits is absent in the search—what is there now in this house of a young hunter?

Who, for a long time, was not deceived by that drop of water held on the tip of a slender blade of grass, mistaking it for a pearl? Alas, this world has its vision inverted; we alone here possess true consciousness.
Even though we reflect upon them in many ways, we do not understand; by what names, then, could we designate those of great intelligence? (Subhāṣitāvalī 982)
For those [fools], the stones are the ultimate authority for discerning the true nature of gold, which is the ornament of the entire world.
While reflecting on this, the farmer cultivated his field to protect it; look, this straw man is his own likeness.
Because he is paralyzed by his lack of action, the herds of wild oxen surely devour the crops right before this fearless man.

O fish, even those two with unblinking eyes, known throughout the world except for the realm of the gods, were indeed caught by you with your mouth opened wide for a morsel; O fool, did you not clearly see this hook within?

"Even if one should fall from manhood, even if one should go to the depths, even if one should not be great in the pursuit of love—even then, such a person shall uplift the entire world. Such a direction has been revealed by some Supreme Person.
The goblin who is a glass merchant stumbles while fashioning nothing more than the conceptual forms of his own family’s craft with his meager intent;
he is consumed within by envy toward the jeweler who effortlessly strings together gems that rival the Kaustubha, the sovereign jewel.
He was maintained as an adversary, yet not properly established as independent; out of fear that he might, being healthy, strike them down, he was not nourished according to his needs.
Let this parched leopard remain here mute; what is the use of him staying in this house? What more need be said? Now, O Householder, mice are prowling about like thieves. (Bhall 78)
If this is so, then how can there be such dullness in the greatness of the nature of passion? And if this is natural passion, why does it possess such a knotted density?
If this Vedic tradition teaches that you are pure at your root, why do you have these defects? O lotus stalk, if these are indeed your qualities, we cannot comprehend your true nature.
Those who are as if smeared with poison, whose crooked ways are such that what more need be said? These double-tongued ones watch for vulnerabilities to destroy the innocent world.
Yet even these serpents, though deluded regarding the true and the false, carry jewels upon their heads; for those endowed with virtue, there is never a lapse from propriety—enough of this worry!

Oh, the cruelty of women! O you who have destroyed the night, shame on you, most treacherous one! This moon—the lord of the eyes of all creatures—has begun his descent into the darkness of the western horizon with his beauty loosened like a disheveled braid; yet you have brought about the end of his affection, a deed worthy only of the dull-witted, such as the oceans and their ilk.
Aha! This lamp, which laughs aloud at night and suffers from the fever of its desire to conquer the day, appropriately withers these false limbs;
moreover, has it even endured the sight of the movement of that darkness which has snatched away the world by its noble and unrestrained advance?
The name of that other tree, which had been closed up, has now been reopened; the hand of Fate itself was seized as it stumbled upon its own path.
And this world has been liberated from the calamity of sight caused by the vision of the undesirable. O woodcutter, it is only right that you have cut down that untimely row of mango trees.

The world was devoured by venomous serpents who subsisted on air alone, having first been comforted [by their asceticism]; those serpents were in turn swallowed by peacocks practicing the severe vow of consuming only drops of rainwater;
even those peacocks were brought to destruction by hunters clad in the skins of cruel deer. Thus, though he knows the manifestation of hypocrisy, the fool still seeks out its virtues.
Alas, what a tragedy! That very white bull—who once bore the great burden all alone upon the most treacherous paths; who never once tolerated the sound of another's bellows in his own pen;
and who was the very ornament of the herd—is now, in his old age, having his price publicly proclaimed for sale. What a pity! (Bhallata 85)

Abandon the suffering of striving for what is impossible; for the sky is not a place fit for the movement of the lame. O virtuous one, this is merely a wicked habit of yours from practicing speed like a moth, leading only to your own exhaustion. Even for the Lord [Viṣṇu], the winds from the tips of Garuḍa’s wings are inconceivable—winds that uproot mountains with effortless play as they traverse the expanse of the world, yet carry the weight of those very mountains along their path.
If the mountain rivers, their waters augmented by the moon and made resonant with the play of waves, were to grant life itself to the ocean;
yet, even when they arrive suddenly, arrogant with pride, he would not diminish otherwise—provided that those very rivers, rendered incapable of providing any remedy, look on like silent witnesses.
It is said that the sage who drank the shoreless ocean with a single handful might drink even a thousand [oceans] without change, were he a glutton;
yet this is not possible. Alas! Without the abode of expanded consciousness, even that which exists remains as if non-existent—the inner radiance of the powerful.

The pressing-stones (*grāvan*) are the ornament here; the three worlds abide within its boundaries. Indeed, it is here that the Moon resides, O gods, having gathered together with their blessings fulfilled.

And here the Lord himself, Brahmā, reclines, shining from the lotus risen from his navel. By fate, even that ocean, though dull-witted, comes to a state of depth for the sake of supporting its own belly.
If my listeners are free from envy, I shall speak; yet one should fear more from one's own side than from a powerful adversary.
For when all-encompassing darkness has descended, these rays of light shine by their own power only when the maker of day is present, and not otherwise.
How much more than that did he hear from his own mouth—that fool who, hearing from him that a drop of water on a lotus leaf was a pearl, thought it so;

yet when that very drop was being taken up slowly by the slight movement of a fingertip, it vanished, and thinking "Where has it flown away? he could not sleep day after day from inner grief. (Bhallata 91)
"Ah, how great is this swan's devotion to contentment! He remains right here in the lake; his mind does not turn even slightly toward a lotus, the abode of beauty.
Even now he sleeps and does not wake; let us wait for him until that time. Thus the bees, who are fond of their bellies, are unable to endure waiting for even a moment longer.
That the frog, croaking with angry harshness, raised his hand without fear to slap the mouth of the black serpent;
and that the serpent, with face turned downward, closed his eyes while remaining there—all this was the playful sport of some Blessed One who is a master of poisons. (Bhall 93)

This bow is drawn wide like the gaping mouth of Death; these arrows have the luster of venomous serpents; his training is such that it has conquered Arjuna and others; his course is downward in every respect;
and oh, what cruelty lies within this rogue! Alas, alas! I think the forest will meet its end just as the sweet and captivating song from the mouth of this hunter shall do for the deer.
What kind of delusion is this of yours, O Wind, that you cause the mass of dust from the trampling of people's feet to find its footing in the sky, which is frequented by hosts of radiant beings?
Let alone the affliction it causes to the path of people's eyes while it is being raised; by what means can this fault of defiling your own body be remedied by you?
These seekers of victory, their gazes fixed upon the doors of kings' palaces, are driven away by gatekeepers arrogant with anger because they set their minds on begging for wealth;
whereas those wise men who paid no heed to riches—finding them tasteless compared to the enjoyment of sense objects—now dwell on the enchanting bank of the celestial river.

Let the winds blow, variegated with the pollen of *kadamba* flowers; let the peacocks—the enemies of serpents—dance; and let the clouds, heavy with the burden of fresh water, release their thunder with vigor.

But you, O lightning, having seen me dejected of face and submerged in the fire of the sorrow of separation from my beloved, why do you flash forth, O pitiless one, even though our commonality as females is equal?

O brother, you who take the lives of those who have surrendered their breaths to you, who have been raised up by you with such force, who were long carried upon your shoulder, and even to whom you offered service—
by producing the destruction of life in an instant with a mere inward smile, you act as the supreme performer of the *vetāla*’s sport among those who repay a favor.
The quarters are stretched out with ropes, the earth is dug up with poison, and the forest edges are ablaze with fire;
hunters with bows in hand are tracking his footprints—where can the leader of the deer herd take refuge?
Thinking, "This is the sole abode of waters" and "This is a mine of jewels," we have resorted to the ocean with minds agitated by thirst.
Who could have known that a sage would, in an instant, drink it up—along with its mass of gasping whales—using the hollow of his own cupped hands?
Seeing the vast flower of the silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*), beautiful to the eye, the parrot thought, "Its fruit might also be like this.
While he sat there for a long time, by fate a fruit ripened; but upon reaching its maturity, it was inside filled with cotton, which was suddenly carried away by the wind.

O Kālakūṭa, how could your birth have been in the ocean—the abode of the Supreme Person (Viṣṇu), which brings benefit to all beings, where all the desires of the renowned gods are fulfilled, and which possesses a splendor spread wide by the mass of the moon’s rays? (Bhallata 102)
When the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*)—its thick branches laden with fruit—dispels the intense radiance of the sun, what creature, even a beast, would seek shade from withered shrubs? || 103 ||
